leaves.label: Ottoman Mother-of-Pearl Inlay
leaves.defn: Ottoman woodwork inlaid with mother-of-pearl, tortoiseshell and ivory (sedefkârlık): Qur'an stands, chests and thrones.
leaves.weak: English sources describe the technique; the Turkish term sedefkârlık is the attested name

leaves.label: Palestinian Olive-Wood Carving
leaves.defn: carved olive wood of Bethlehem and Jerusalem, devotional and souvenir objects since the 16th century.
src: Wikidata Q7087239 (Olive wood carving in Palestine)

leaves.label: Islamic Woodwork
leaves.defn: carved and joined woodwork of the Islamic world outside the named leaves: minbars, Qur'an stands and cenotaphs carved in bevelled and geometric strapwork (the Minbar of Nur al-Din, Aleppo 1168).
leaves.weak: a broad leaf for woodwork outside named traditions; split when the field names its schools
alias_rows: Abu al-Hasan Walidi Waladay Yahya al-Halabi

leaves.label: ʿAjami
leaves.defn: painted, gessoed and gilded wooden panelling of Ottoman Syrian reception rooms (the Aleppo Room, 1600–03; the Damascus Room, 1707).

leaves.label: Kondapalli Toys
leaves.defn: Carved and painted softwood (tella poniki) figures of Kondapalli in Andhra Pradesh: Dasavatara sets, ambari elephant.

leaves.label: Nirmal Toys
leaves.defn: Painted softwood toys and lacquered paintings of the Naqqash families of Nirmal in Telangana.

leaves.label: Malay Woodcarving
leaves.defn: The carved wood of the Malay Peninsula, above all of Kelantan and Terengganu, for palaces, houses, boats and weapon hilts, in pierced floral (awan larat) designs.

leaves.label: Yosegi-zaiku
leaves.defn: Wood mosaic of Hakone: blocks of differently coloured woods glued into patterns and planed into veneers for boxes and puzzle boxes.

leaves.label: Ainu Woodcarving
leaves.defn: Ainu carving of wood in curving and scale designs: prayer sticks (ikupasuy), trays, knife hilts (makiri) and ritual objects, and the carved trays of Nibutani.

leaves.label: Hwagak
leaves.defn: Korean painted ox-horn veneer: thin translucent horn sheets painted on the back in bright colours and laid on boxes and furniture; makers designated hwagakjang.

leaves.label: Mate Burilado
leaves.defn: Engraved and pyrographed gourds of the central Peruvian Andes (Huanta, Cochas Chico), with dense narrative scenes.

leaves.label: Bentwood Boxes
leaves.defn: Kerfed, steamed and bent cedar boxes and chests of the Northwest Coast, carved and painted in formline: storage and grease boxes, bentwood chests, bent-corner bowls.

leaves.label: Fijian Clubs
leaves.defn: The carved hardwood war clubs (i-wau) of Fiji, made by specialist carvers in named forms and often finely incised: totokia (pineapple club), gata (gunstock club), i-ula throwing clubs, kinikini paddle clubs.

leaves.label: Tramp Art
leaves.defn: American and European woodwork of c. 1870–1940 built up from notch-carved layers of cigar-box and crate wood: boxes, frames, miniature furniture.

leaves.label: Abramtsevo-Kudrino Carving
leaves.defn: Flat relief wood carving of curling floral ornament on boxes, ladles and furniture, created at the Abramtsevo estate workshop by Vasily Vornoskov of Kudrino (late 19th century) and continued at Khotkovo.

leaves.label: Untsukul Inlay
leaves.defn: Woodwork of the Avar village of Untsukul (Dagestan) inlaid with fine silver and cupronickel wire and plates in geometric patterns: walking sticks, boxes, vases.
leaves.weak: attestation weak (news page)

leaves.label: Hutsul Wood Carving
leaves.defn: Carving and inlay of the Hutsuls of the Ukrainian Carpathians — chip carving, beadwork inlay and brass inlay on boxes, plates and crosses (Shkriblyak family).

leaves.label: Chernihiv Wood Carving
leaves.defn: Traditional artistic wood carving of Chernihiv Oblast (Ukraine).
leaves.aliases: artistic wood carving of Chernihiv Oblast

leaves.label: Konjic Woodcarving
leaves.defn: Woodcarving of Konjic in Bosnia and Herzegovina, with dense floral and geometric relief on furniture and interiors (UNESCO 2017).

leaves.label: Kuksa
leaves.defn: Carved drinking cups of birch burl made by the Sámi and Finns.

leaves.label: Boulle Work
leaves.defn: Marquetry of tortoiseshell and brass (with pewter and horn) cut together in première- and contre-partie sheets, perfected for Louis XIV's court by André-Charles Boulle and revived in the 19th century: Boulle commodes for the Trianon, bracket clocks and pedestals, bureaux plats.

leaves.label: Persian Lacquer
leaves.defn: painted and varnished papier-mâché and wood of Iran — pen boxes, mirror cases, bindings and caskets — from the Timurid and Safavid periods to its Zand and Qajar flowering (Muhammad Zaman, 'Ali Ashraf, Muhammad Isma'il).
leaves.see: C3-1 Islamic Bookbinding; A1-2 Persian Miniature.

leaves.label: Kashmiri Papier-Mâché
leaves.defn: painted and varnished papier-mâché of Kashmir (boxes, vases), with floral and hunting designs.

leaves.label: Edirnekâri
leaves.defn: Ottoman lacquer of Edirne (17th–19th century): writing boxes, bookbindings and furniture painted with flowers under varnish.
leaves.weak: attested in Turkish sources (Edirnekâri); English sources say Ottoman lacquer

leaves.label: Channapatna Toys
leaves.defn: Lathe-turned wooden toys of Channapatna in Karnataka finished in coloured lac.

leaves.label: Etikoppaka Toys
leaves.defn: Lac-turned wooden toys of Etikoppaka in Andhra Pradesh coloured with vegetable dyes.

leaves.label: Burmese Lacquerware
leaves.defn: Coiled-bamboo and horsehair vessels coated in thitsi lacquer, engraved (yun) or gilded and glass-inlaid, made above all in Bagan: offering vessels (hsun-ok), betel boxes, manuscript chests.

leaves.label: Lai Rot Nam
leaves.defn: Thai gold-and-black lacquer decoration on wood, made by gold leaf on a lacquer ground with a water-washed resist: manuscript cabinets, temple doors and window shutters.

leaves.label: Carved Lacquer
leaves.defn: Chinese lacquer built up in many layers and carved in relief, from the Song: tihong cinnabar lacquer, tixi guri scrolls, Yongle and Qianlong imperial boxes.

leaves.label: Maki-e
leaves.defn: Japanese lacquer decorated with sprinkled gold and silver powder, from the Heian period: Kōdaiji maki-e, Hon'ami Kōetsu's writing boxes, inrō, Nanban export lacquer.

leaves.label: Japanese Lacquerware
leaves.defn: Japanese lacquer other than maki-e, made in regional centres named for their wares: Wajima-nuri, Tsugaru-nuri, Kamakura-bori, Negoro, and raden mother-of-pearl inlay.

leaves.label: Ryukyuan Lacquerware
leaves.defn: Lacquer of the Ryukyu kingdom (15th–19th century) with red grounds, mother-of-pearl inlay, gold-leaf (chinkin) and relief (tsuikin) decoration.

leaves.label: Najeonchilgi
leaves.defn: Korean lacquer inlaid with mother-of-pearl, from Goryeo sutra boxes to Joseon clothing chests; makers designated najeonjang and chiljang.

leaves.label: Yi Lacquerware
leaves.defn: Red, yellow and black painted lacquer of the Yi (Nuosu) of Liangshan in Sichuan: wooden bowls, cups and armour.
leaves.weak: scholarly article on Liangshan Yi lacquerware (national ICH); no Wikipedia article

leaves.label: Kintsugi
leaves.defn: Japanese repair of broken ceramics with lacquer dusted with gold, valued as an aesthetic in its own right since the 16th century.

leaves.label: Mexican Lacquerware
leaves.defn: Lacquer (maque) of Mexico made with insect and seed-oil lacquers on gourds and wood, by inlay or painting, in its regional centres: Olinalá boxes, Pátzcuaro gilded trays, Chiapa de Corzo gourds.

leaves.label: Barniz de Pasto
leaves.defn: Decoration of wood with sheets of mopa-mopa resin cut and applied in colour, practised in Pasto (Nariño) since the colonial period (UNESCO urgent safeguarding 2020).

leaves.label: Khokhloma
leaves.defn: Painted and varnished turned woodenware of the Nizhny Novgorod region (Semyonov, Khokhloma) since the 17th century, with red and black foliage over a gold-like ground produced by tin powder and oven-hardened varnish: bowls, spoons, ladles.

leaves.label: Palekh Miniature
leaves.defn: Lacquer miniature painting in egg tempera on black papier-mâché boxes from Palekh, created by former icon painters in 1923 (Golikov), with fairy-tale scenes in gold.

leaves.label: Fedoskino Miniature
leaves.defn: Lacquer miniature painting in oils on papier-mâché from Fedoskino near Moscow since 1795 (Lukutin factory), with genre scenes over mother-of-pearl and metal-leaf grounds.

leaves.label: Mstyora Miniature
leaves.defn: Lacquer miniature painting of Mstyora (Vladimir region) from 1923, with landscapes in warm tones and gold ornament on papier-mâché.

leaves.label: Kholuy Miniature
leaves.defn: Lacquer miniature painting of Kholuy (Ivanovo region) from 1934, by former icon painters, with dense narrative scenes in blue and green.

subs.label: Furniture & Decorative Arts Styles
subs.axis: Axis: period style of furniture and the decorative arts (Louis XIV to Mid-Century Modern); designers and makers are kinds.

leaves.label: Soban
leaves.defn: Korean small portable dining tables of wood in regional styles (Naju, Haeju, Tongyeong); makers designated sobanjang.

leaves.label: Queen Anne Style (furniture)
leaves.defn: English and American furniture of c. 1700–1755 with cabriole legs, pad and claw-and-ball feet, shell carving and walnut veneers, continuing in the colonies after Queen Anne's reign: Philadelphia and Newport high chests, vase-splat side chairs, bonnet-top highboys.
leaves.aliases: Queen Anne furniture;Queen Anne style furniture
leaves.see: I3-5 Louis XV Style;I3-3 Chippendale Furniture;K2-19 Queen Anne Style Architecture

leaves.label: Chippendale Furniture
leaves.defn: English and American furniture of c. 1750–1790 after Thomas Chippendale's pattern book The Gentleman and Cabinet-Maker's Director (1754), in Rococo, Gothic and Chinese taste in mahogany: Director plates, ribbon-back chairs, Philadelphia Chippendale high chests, Newport block-front desks.
leaves.see: I3-2 Queen Anne Style (furniture);I3-4 Hepplewhite Style;I3-5 Louis XV Style
leaves.weak: 'Chippendale furniture' is a Wikipedia redirect to Thomas Chippendale; 42 Director plates in the Smithsonian evidence

leaves.label: Hepplewhite Style
leaves.defn: English and American Neoclassical furniture of c. 1775–1800 after George Hepplewhite's Cabinet-Maker and Upholsterer's Guide (1788): shield- and heart-back chairs, square tapering legs, inlaid satinwood: shield-back chairs, Federal sideboards with spade feet.
leaves.see: I3-5 Sheraton Style;I3-6 Louis XVI Style;I3-3 Chippendale Furniture
leaves.weak: 'Hepplewhite style' redirects to George Hepplewhite; Hepplewhite himself now sits in I3-6 Louis XVI Style

leaves.label: Sheraton Style
leaves.defn: English and American late Neoclassical furniture of c. 1790–1820 after Thomas Sheraton's Cabinet-Maker and Upholsterer's Drawing-Book (1791–94): straight lines, turned and reeded legs, painted and inlaid satinwood: Drawing-Book designs, square-back chairs, Duncan Phyfe's early work.
leaves.see: I3-4 Hepplewhite Style;I3-7 Empire Style;I3-6 Louis XVI Style

leaves.label: International Gothic (decorative arts)
leaves.defn: Courtly late Gothic goldsmiths' work, tapestry and glass (c. 1250–1450): the Goldenes Rössl, the Apocalypse Tapestry of Angers.

leaves.label: Mannerism (decorative arts)
leaves.defn: Renaissance and Mannerist decorative arts and ornament (c. 1450–1600): Cellini's Salt Cellar, Jamnitzer's goldsmiths' work, Pannemaker's tapestries.

leaves.label: Louis XIV Style
leaves.defn: French court decorative arts c. 1660–1715 under Le Brun: Boulle marquetry, Gobelins tapestries, Versailles silver furniture.

leaves.label: Louis XV Style
leaves.defn: The Rococo decorative arts of France c. 1715–1760: Cressent's commodes, Meissonnier's ornament, Vincennes-Sèvres porcelain.
leaves.see: T161 Louis XIV Style;T163 Louis XVI Style

leaves.label: Louis XVI Style
leaves.defn: Early neoclassical decorative arts in France c. 1760–1790: Riesener's furniture, Marie-Antoinette's boudoir at Fontainebleau.
leaves.see: T162 Louis XV Style;T164 Empire Style

leaves.label: Empire Style
leaves.defn: Napoleonic neoclassical design c. 1800–1830: Percier and Fontaine's Malmaison, Jacob-Desmalter's furniture.

leaves.label: Biedermeier
leaves.defn: Central European design and domestic culture 1815–1848, simple and comfortable, and its painting of bourgeois life: Danhauser furniture, Waldmüller's genre scenes.
leaves.see: T164 Empire Style;T166 Victorian Decorative Arts

leaves.label: Victorian Decorative Arts
leaves.defn: British decorative arts 1837–1901, historicist and industrial: Pugin's Gothic Revival furniture, Minton majolica.

leaves.label: Arts and Crafts Movement
leaves.defn: The reform of design and craft after Ruskin and Morris (1860s–1920s): Morris & Co. wallpapers, Ashbee's silver, Stickley's Craftsman furniture.

leaves.label: Art Nouveau
leaves.defn: The international style of organic line and ornament c. 1890–1910 across design, architecture and painting: Gallé's glass, Mucha's posters, Horta's Hôtel Tassel, Klimt's Beethoven Frieze.
leaves.see: T169 Art Deco;T185 Art Nouveau Architecture;T53 Symbolism

leaves.label: Art Deco
leaves.defn: The streamlined geometric luxury style of the 1920s–1930s: Ruhlmann's furniture, Lalique glass, Cassandre's posters, the Chrysler Building.

leaves.label: Bauhaus
leaves.defn: The German school of art and design (1919–1933) and its functional modernism: Breuer's Wassily Chair, Brandt's tea infuser, Albers's weavings.
leaves.see: T169 Art Deco;T172 Mid-Century Modern;T65 Constructivism

leaves.label: Mingei
leaves.defn: The Japanese folk-craft movement (1926) of Yanagi Sōetsu, Hamada and Kawai: Hamada Shōji's stoneware, Serizawa Keisuke's stencil dyeing.
leaves.see: T167 Arts and Crafts Movement;E3 Stoneware

leaves.label: Mid-Century Modern
leaves.defn: Modern design c. 1933–1965: the Eames Lounge Chair, Arne Jacobsen's Egg chair, Castiglioni lamps.

leaves.label: Contemporary Design
leaves.defn: Design by makers born from 1945: product, furniture, fashion and graphic design.

subs.label: Musical Instruments
subs.axis: Axis: tradition. Instruments studied as decorated objects, whatever their material.

leaves.label: Vanuatu Slit Gongs
leaves.defn: The upright slit gongs of northern Vanuatu (Ambrym, Malakula), breadfruit trunks hollowed and carved with ancestral faces and raised in dancing grounds of the grade societies: atingting kon (Ambrym), Malakula slit gongs; tree-fern grade figures as a kind.

fams.label: Photography
fams.test: an image made with a camera. Photographers and artists are kinds of their school or movement.

subs.label: Photographic Schools & Movements
subs.axis: Axis: period style and movement (pictorialism, straight photography, documentary, contemporary).

leaves.label: Modernist Photography
leaves.defn: The period style of photographers born c. 1860–1944 working in the modern idioms of the 20th century outside a recorded school: sharp-focus, experimental and illustrated-press photography between Pictorialism and the contemporary generation: Stieglitz's The Steerage, Kertész's Fork, Sudek's Prague views.
leaves.see: J1-3 Straight Photography;J1-4 New Vision;J1-6 Documentary Photography;J1-7 Contemporary Photography;A5-110 Modern Art

leaves.label: Street Photography
leaves.defn: Candid photography of chance encounters in public places, mostly with the hand-held camera, from 1930s Paris and New York to the 1960s American and Japanese street: Levitt's children's chalk drawings, Frank's The Americans, Winogrand's Women Are Beautiful, Moriyama's Stray Dog.
leaves.see: J1-5 Humanistic Photography;J1-6 Documentary Photography;J1-3 Photojournalism

leaves.label: Photojournalism
leaves.defn: Photography made to report news for the illustrated press, from the Weimar picture magazines and Life to war and agency photography: Capa's Falling Soldier, Rosenthal's Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima, Eddie Adams's Saigon Execution, Nick Ut's The Terror of War.

leaves.label: Surrealist Photography
leaves.defn: Photography of the Surrealist movement and its circles, 1920s–1950s, using rayographs, solarisation, staged mannequins and found street images: Man Ray's Rayographs, Boiffard's Big Toe, Bellmer's La Poupée, Grete Stern's Sueños.

leaves.label: Fashion Photography
leaves.defn: Photography of clothing and models for fashion magazines and advertising, from de Meyer and Steichen at Vogue to the Avedon–Penn generation and the 1960s London and Paris photographers: Steichen's Art of the Gown (1911), Horst's Mainbocher Corset, Avedon's Dovima with Elephants, Penn's Harlequin Dress.

leaves.label: Düsseldorf School of Photography
leaves.defn: The students of Bernd and Hilla Becher at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf from 1976, making serial, frontal and large-format colour photographs: the Bechers' Water Towers typologies, Gursky's 99 Cent, Struth's Museum Photographs, Ruff's Portraits.
leaves.see: J1-7 Contemporary Photography;A5-34 Düsseldorf School of Painting

leaves.label: Early Photography
leaves.defn: Photography of the daguerreotype, calotype and wet-collodion decades (1839–c. 1880): Talbot's The Open Door, Nadar's portraits, Cameron's portraits.

leaves.label: Pictorialism
leaves.defn: The first international art-photography movement (1880s–1920s), soft-focus and hand-worked: Steichen's The Pond—Moonlight, Käsebier's Blessed Art Thou among Women.

leaves.label: Straight Photography
leaves.defn: Sharp-focus, unmanipulated modernist photography from the 1910s (Group f/64): Strand's Wall Street, Weston's Pepper No. 30, Adams's Moonrise, Hernandez.

leaves.label: New Vision
leaves.defn: The experimental photography of the 1920s–1930s (Neues Sehen) of angles, close-ups and photograms: Moholy-Nagy's photograms, Rodchenko's Pioneer Girl.

leaves.label: Humanistic Photography
leaves.defn: French post-war photography of everyday life and its dignity: Doisneau's Kiss by the Hôtel de Ville, Willy Ronis's Le Petit Parisien.

leaves.label: Documentary Photography
leaves.defn: Photography that records people, places and events for social or historical purpose, including photojournalism: Lange's Migrant Mother, Evans's Let Us Now Praise Famous Men, Salgado's Workers.

leaves.label: Contemporary Photography
leaves.defn: Photography by artists born from 1945, staged, documentary and conceptual.

fams.label: Architecture
fams.test: a building or designed built whole, placed by its style; buildings are representative works and architects are kinds.
key: 1. A revival built outside the tradition it revives? → K2 (P8).
2. A style of the Islamic world? → K1.

3. Otherwise the style's own tradition: ancient Mediterranean and Near East → K3; medieval Europe → K4; Europe and its colonies 1400–1850 → K5; modern and contemporary movements → K6; South Asia → K7; East Asia → K8; Southeast Asia → K9; Africa → K10; the Indigenous Americas → K11; named vernacular and Oceanic traditions → K12.

subs.label: Islamic Architecture
subs.axis: Axis: the dynastic and regional style named by architectural history; sub-styles and architects are its kinds.

leaves.label: Umayyad Architecture
leaves.defn: the architecture of the Umayyad caliphate (661–750): the Dome of the Rock, the Great Mosque of Damascus and the desert palaces (Qusayr 'Amra, Khirbat al-Mafjar, Mshatta).
leaves.see: L3-1 Umayyad Mosaics; L2-1 Umayyad Wall Painting.

leaves.label: Abbasid Architecture
leaves.defn: the architecture of the Abbasid caliphate (750–1258): Samarra's mosques and palaces, the round city of Baghdad and the Tulunid mosque of Cairo.

leaves.label: Fatimid Architecture
leaves.defn: the architecture of the Fatimid caliphate in Ifriqiya and Egypt (909–1171): al-Azhar, al-Hakim and the gates of Cairo.

leaves.label: Moorish Architecture
leaves.defn: the Islamic architecture of al-Andalus and the Maghreb: the caliphal Great Mosque of Córdoba and Madinat al-Zahra, the taifa Aljafería, Almoravid and Almohad mosques and the Nasrid Alhambra.
leaves.see: K1-5 Mudéjar Architecture; K2-1 Moorish Revival Architecture.

leaves.label: Mudéjar Architecture
leaves.defn: the Islamic-derived architecture built under Christian rule in Iberia (12th–16th century), in brick, tile and carpentry (artesonado ceilings).

leaves.label: Seljuk Architecture
leaves.defn: the architecture of the Great Seljuqs in Iran and Central Asia (11th–12th century): four-iwan mosques, domed chambers, brick tomb towers and minarets.

leaves.label: Anatolian Seljuk Architecture
leaves.defn: the architecture of the Seljuqs of Rum and the beyliks in Anatolia (12th–14th century): caravanserais, madrasas with carved stone portals, and tomb towers.

leaves.label: Mamluk Architecture
leaves.defn: the architecture of the Mamluk sultanate in Egypt and Syria (1250–1517): funerary complexes with domes and minarets, ablaq masonry and carved stone domes.
leaves.see: K1-3 Fatimid Architecture; K2-3 Neo-Mamluk Architecture.

leaves.label: Ilkhanid Architecture
leaves.defn: the architecture of the Mongol Ilkhanate in Iran (1256–1335): the Mausoleum of Öljeitü at Soltaniyeh and great mosques with tiled portals.

leaves.label: Timurid Architecture
leaves.defn: the architecture of Timur and his successors in Central Asia and Iran (1370–1507): Samarkand, Herat and Mashhad, with bulbous ribbed domes and tile-mosaic revetment.

leaves.label: Safavid Architecture
leaves.defn: the architecture of Safavid Iran (1501–1736), above all Isfahan's Naqsh-e Jahan square, its mosques, palaces and bridges.

leaves.label: Ottoman Architecture
leaves.defn: the architecture of the Ottoman empire from the early Bursa and Edirne mosques through the classical domed mosques of Mimar Sinan to Ottoman Baroque.
leaves.see: K1-7 Anatolian Seljuk Architecture; K2-4 First National Architectural Movement.

leaves.label: Qajar Architecture
leaves.defn: the architecture of Qajar Iran (1789–1925): palaces and mosques with polychrome figural tiles (Golestan Palace).

leaves.label: Indo-Islamic Architecture
leaves.defn: the Islamic architecture of the South Asian sultanates before and beside the Mughals: Delhi Sultanate (Qutb Minar), Gujarat, Bengal, Malwa and the Deccan sultanates.

leaves.label: Mughal Architecture
leaves.defn: the architecture of the Mughal empire (1526–1857): Humayun's tomb, Fatehpur Sikri, the Taj Mahal and the Mughal gardens.

leaves.label: Sudano-Sahelian Architecture
leaves.defn: the earthen architecture of the West African Sahel: mud-brick mosques with projecting torons (Djenné, Timbuktu, Agadez).

leaves.label: Swahili Architecture
leaves.defn: the coral-stone architecture of the Swahili coast (Kilwa, Lamu, Zanzibar): mosques, pillar tombs and carved doors.

leaves.label: Chinese Islamic Architecture
leaves.defn: mosques of China in the Chinese timber-frame idiom (Xi'an, Niujie) and the brick and tiled mosques of Xinjiang.

leaves.label: Javanese Mosque Architecture
leaves.defn: the mosques of Java and the Malay world built in the regional timber idiom with stacked pyramidal (tajug) roofs instead of domes (Demak, Kudus, Menara Kudus).
leaves.see: K1-18 Chinese Islamic Architecture; C2-4 Malay Manuscripts.
leaves.weak: attested through its buildings (Demak, Kudus); no item for the style name itself

subs.label: Historicist & National Revivals
subs.axis: Axis: the style revived. Built at scale; the pilot holds the revivals of Islamic styles.

leaves.label: Moorish Revival Architecture
leaves.defn: the 19th–20th-century revival of Moorish and Islamic forms in Europe and the Americas — synagogues, theatres, baths and palaces.

leaves.label: Neo-Mudéjar
leaves.defn: the Spanish revival of Mudéjar brick and tile (late 19th–early 20th century): bullrings, stations and schools.

leaves.label: Neo-Mamluk Architecture
leaves.defn: the revival of Mamluk forms in Egypt and beyond (late 19th–20th century).

leaves.label: First National Architectural Movement
leaves.defn: the Turkish national style of 1908–1930 reviving Ottoman and Seljuq forms (Vedat Tek, Mimar Kemaleddin).

leaves.label: Indo-Saracenic Architecture
leaves.defn: the British colonial revival style in India (from the 1870s) combining Indo-Islamic and Mughal forms with Gothic and Neoclassical planning: railway stations, courts and palaces (Robert Fellowes Chisholm, Charles Mant).
leaves.see: K1-15 Mughal Architecture; K2-1 Moorish Revival Architecture.

leaves.label: Gothic Revival Architecture
leaves.defn: The revival of medieval Gothic forms from the mid-18th century to the early 20th, in churches, colleges, parliaments and houses: the Palace of Westminster, Cologne Cathedral's completion, St Patrick's Cathedral, New York.
leaves.see: T181 Gothic Architecture; K2-7 Tudor Revival Architecture

leaves.label: Tudor Revival Architecture
leaves.defn: The revival of Tudor and Elizabethan domestic forms (half-timbering, tall chimneys, mullioned windows) in late 19th- and 20th-century houses: Jacobethan country houses, mock-Tudor suburban villas.
leaves.see: K5-1 Tudor Architecture; K2-6 Gothic Revival Architecture

leaves.label: Romanesque Revival Architecture
leaves.defn: The 19th-century revival of round-arched Romanesque forms, from the German Rundbogenstil to Richardsonian Romanesque in America: Trinity Church, Boston, the Natural History Museum, London.
leaves.see: K4-10 Romanesque Architecture; K2-9 Neo-Byzantine Architecture

leaves.label: Neo-Byzantine Architecture
leaves.defn: The 19th–20th-century revival of Byzantine domes, arcades and banded masonry, in Orthodox and Catholic churches and public buildings: Sacré-Cœur, Paris, Westminster Cathedral, Saint Sava, Belgrade.
leaves.see: K4-2 Byzantine Architecture; K2-27 Russian Revival Architecture

leaves.label: Renaissance Revival Architecture
leaves.defn: The 19th-century revival of Italian, French and Northern Renaissance forms for palaces, banks, museums and civic buildings: the Vienna State Opera, the Reform Club, the Rijksmuseum.
leaves.see: T182 Renaissance Architecture; K2-11 Italianate Architecture; K2-12 Second Empire Style

leaves.label: Italianate Architecture
leaves.defn: The 19th-century picturesque revival of Italian villa and palazzo forms, with bracketed eaves and towers, popular in Britain and North America: Osborne House, Italianate row houses of San Francisco.

leaves.label: Second Empire Style
leaves.defn: The Napoleon III-era style of mansard roofs and rich Baroque-Renaissance ornament, spread from Paris to the Americas: the Palais Garnier, Philadelphia City Hall, the Eisenhower Executive Office Building.
leaves.aliases: Napoleon III style; Second Empire architecture
leaves.see: K2-10 Renaissance Revival Architecture; K2-16 Beaux-Arts Architecture
alias_rows: Second Empire architecture in the United States and Canada

leaves.label: Baroque Revival Architecture
leaves.defn: The late 19th- and early 20th-century revival of Baroque massing and ornament for public buildings and theatres: the Berlin Cathedral, Edwardian Baroque town halls.
leaves.see: T183 Baroque Architecture; K2-16 Beaux-Arts Architecture

leaves.label: Greek Revival Architecture
leaves.defn: The late 18th- and 19th-century revival of Greek temple forms and orders, dominant in the United States and northern Europe: the Second Bank of the United States, the Altes Museum, St George's Hall, Liverpool.
leaves.see: T184 Neoclassical Architecture; K3-8 Ancient Greek Architecture

leaves.label: Egyptian Revival Architecture
leaves.defn: The revival of ancient Egyptian pylons, obelisks and lotus columns after Napoleon's Egyptian campaign, in cemeteries, prisons, synagogues and cinemas: the Egyptian Hall, Piccadilly, the Tombs, New York.

leaves.label: Beaux-Arts Architecture
leaves.defn: The academic classical architecture taught at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris (c. 1830–1920), symmetrical and richly sculpted, carried to the Americas: the Petit Palais, New York Public Library, Grand Central Terminal.
leaves.see: K2-12 Second Empire Style; K2-17 Eclecticism in Architecture

leaves.label: Eclecticism in Architecture
leaves.defn: Nineteenth- and early 20th-century architecture freely combining historical styles in one building: Gründerzeit apartment blocks, Stile Umbertino palaces of Rome, Russian eclectic mansions.
leaves.see: K2-16 Beaux-Arts Architecture; K2-18 Victorian Architecture

leaves.label: Victorian Architecture
leaves.defn: The succession of revival and picturesque styles built in Britain and its empire and in North America during Victoria's reign (1837–1901): Stick style houses, Eastlake villas, Australian Victorian terraces.
leaves.see: K2-6 Gothic Revival Architecture; K2-19 Queen Anne Style Architecture; K2-33 Federation Architecture

leaves.label: Queen Anne Style Architecture
leaves.defn: The late 19th-century British and American domestic style of red brick or shingle, asymmetrical towers, bays and turrets: Norman Shaw's Swan House, the Carson Mansion.
leaves.see: K2-18 Victorian Architecture; K2-20 Shingle Style Architecture
alias_rows: Queen Anne style architecture in the United States

leaves.label: Shingle Style Architecture
leaves.defn: The American seaside and suburban house style of the 1880s wrapped in continuous wood shingles: the Isaac Bell House, the William Watts Sherman House.
leaves.see: K2-19 Queen Anne Style Architecture; K2-21 Colonial Revival Architecture

leaves.label: Colonial Revival Architecture
leaves.defn: The American (and Brazilian) revival from the 1876 Centennial of colonial Georgian and Dutch forms: Georgian Revival houses, Dutch Colonial Revival gambrel houses.
leaves.see: K5-15 American Colonial Architecture; K5-10 Georgian Architecture

leaves.label: Spanish Colonial Revival Architecture
leaves.defn: The early 20th-century revival of Spanish colonial forms in California, Florida and the American Southwest, after the 1915 Panama–California Exposition: Santa Barbara County Courthouse, the California Building, San Diego.
leaves.see: K5-16 Spanish Colonial Architecture; K2-23 Mission Revival Architecture

leaves.label: Mission Revival Architecture
leaves.defn: The Californian revival (1890–1920) of the Spanish missions' arcades, curved parapets and bell towers: the Mission Inn, Riverside, the Santa Fe Depot, San Diego.

leaves.label: Pueblo Revival Architecture
leaves.defn: The 20th-century revival in New Mexico and Arizona of Pueblo and Spanish adobe forms: the New Mexico Museum of Art, La Fonda on the Plaza.

leaves.label: Mayan Revival Architecture
leaves.defn: The 1920s–1930s American revival of Maya and Mesoamerican ornament: Frank Lloyd Wright's Hollyhock House, the Mayan Theater, Los Angeles.

leaves.label: Neo-Manueline
leaves.defn: The Portuguese and Brazilian revival (from the 1840s) of Manueline ornament: Pena Palace, Rossio Station, the Royal Portuguese Cabinet of Reading, Rio.

leaves.label: Russian Revival Architecture
leaves.defn: The 19th-century revival of medieval Muscovite and Byzantine-Russian forms in the Russian Empire: the State Historical Museum, the Church of the Savior on Blood, the Upper Trading Rows.

leaves.label: Russian Neoclassical Revival
leaves.defn: The revival of Russian Neoclassicism and Empire style in the Russian Empire c. 1900–1917 (retrospectivism): Fomin's Polovtsov Dacha, Zholtovsky's Tarasov House.
leaves.see: K5-11 Empire Style; T184 Neoclassical Architecture

leaves.label: Romanian Revival Architecture
leaves.defn: The Romanian national style (from the 1880s) reviving Brâncovenesc and Moldavian forms: Ion Mincu's Lahovari House, Mincu's Bufetul de la Șosea.

leaves.label: National Romantic Style
leaves.defn: The Nordic and Baltic national architecture of c. 1890–1920 drawing on vernacular and medieval forms: Helsinki Central Station, Stockholm City Hall, Norwegian dragestil.
leaves.see: T185 Art Nouveau Architecture; K2-31 Zakopane Style

leaves.label: Zakopane Style
leaves.defn: The Polish national style created by Stanisław Witkiewicz (1890s) from Podhale highland timber building: Villa Koliba, the Chapel in Jaszczurówka.

leaves.label: Swiss Chalet Style
leaves.defn: The 19th-century picturesque revival of the Alpine timber chalet, built across Europe and Scandinavia: Norwegian sveitserstil villas, spa pavilions.

leaves.label: Federation Architecture
leaves.defn: The Australian architecture of c. 1890–1915, combining Queen Anne, Arts and Crafts and Romanesque elements: Federation Queen Anne houses, the Queen Victoria Building.
leaves.see: K2-18 Victorian Architecture; K2-19 Queen Anne Style Architecture

leaves.label: Rustic Architecture
leaves.defn: The North American log-and-stone style of the Adirondack Great Camps and the national parks (1870s–1940s): Old Faithful Inn, Timberline Lodge.

subs.label: Ancient Mediterranean & Near Eastern Architecture
subs.axis: Axis: the civilisation's style (Egyptian, Mesopotamian, Greek orders, Roman).

leaves.label: Ancient Egyptian Architecture
leaves.defn: The stone architecture of pharaonic Egypt (c. 3000 BC – AD 300): pyramids, temples and rock-cut tombs: the Pyramids of Giza, Karnak, Abu Simbel.

leaves.label: Architecture of Mesopotamia
leaves.defn: The mud-brick architecture of Sumer, Babylonia and Assyria: ziggurats, temples, palaces and city walls: the Ziggurat of Ur, the Ishtar Gate, the palaces of Nimrud.
leaves.aliases: Mesopotamian architecture; Assyrian architecture; Babylonian architecture

leaves.label: Achaemenid Architecture
leaves.defn: The palace and tomb architecture of the Persian empire (550–330 BC): Persepolis, Pasargadae, Naqsh-e Rostam.
leaves.see: K3-2 Architecture of Mesopotamia; K3-4 Parthian Architecture

leaves.label: Parthian Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of the Arsacid empire (247 BC – AD 224), with the first monumental iwans and Hellenistic ornament: Hatra, Nisa, Ashur's Parthian palace.
leaves.see: K3-3 Achaemenid Architecture; K3-5 Sasanian Architecture
leaves.weak: enwiki title Parthian architecture checked: redirects to Parthian style (Pope); label attested by QID; 25 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

leaves.label: Sasanian Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of the Sasanian empire (224–651): vaulted iwans, squinch domes and fire temples: Taq Kasra, Palace of Ardashir, Takht-e Soleyman.

leaves.label: Minoan Architecture
leaves.defn: The Bronze Age palace architecture of Crete (c. 2000–1450 BC): Knossos, Phaistos, Malia.
leaves.weak: enwiki Minoan architecture checked: redirects to Minoan civilization#Architecture; 0 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

leaves.label: Mycenaean Architecture
leaves.defn: The Late Bronze Age citadels, megara and tholos tombs of mainland Greece: the Lion Gate, Mycenae, the Treasury of Atreus, Tiryns.
leaves.see: K3-6 Minoan Architecture; K3-8 Ancient Greek Architecture
leaves.weak: enwiki Mycenaean architecture checked: redirects to Mycenaean Greece#Architecture; 3 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

leaves.label: Ancient Greek Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of the Greek world from the Archaic to the Hellenistic period, defined by the temple and the orders: the Parthenon, the Temple of Hephaestus, the Theatre of Epidaurus.
leaves.see: K3-10 Ancient Roman Architecture; K2-14 Greek Revival Architecture

leaves.label: Etruscan Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of the Etruscans (c. 900–27 BC): timber-and-terracotta temples, arched gates and rock-cut tombs: the Banditaccia necropolis, the Arch of Augustus, Perugia.

leaves.label: Ancient Roman Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of Rome and its empire (c. 500 BC – AD 400), of the arch, vault, dome and concrete: the Pantheon, the Colosseum, the Pont du Gard.
leaves.see: K3-8 Ancient Greek Architecture; K4-1 Early Christian Architecture

leaves.label: Nabataean Architecture
leaves.defn: The rock-cut tomb and temple façades of the Nabataeans (1st century BC – 2nd century AD): Al-Khazneh, Ad Deir at Petra, Hegra.

subs.label: Medieval European Architecture
subs.axis: Axis: period style (Byzantine, Romanesque, Gothic and their regional schools).

leaves.label: Early Christian Architecture
leaves.defn: The church architecture of the late Roman empire (4th–6th century): basilicas, baptisteries and martyria: Old St Peter's, Santa Sabina, the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia.
leaves.aliases: Early Christian art and architecture; Paleochristian architecture
leaves.see: K3-10 Ancient Roman Architecture; K4-2 Byzantine Architecture
leaves.weak: enwiki Early Christian architecture checked: redirects to Early Christian art and architecture; 87 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

leaves.label: Byzantine Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of the Eastern Roman empire (c. 330–1453): domed churches on pendentives and the cross-in-square plan: Hagia Sophia, San Vitale, Ravenna, Hosios Loukas.
leaves.see: K4-1 Early Christian Architecture; K2-9 Neo-Byzantine Architecture; K4-3 Serbo-Byzantine Architecture

leaves.label: Serbo-Byzantine Architecture
leaves.defn: The medieval church architecture of Serbia (12th–15th century) in its Raška, Vardar and Morava schools: Studenica, Gračanica, Ravanica.

leaves.label: Architecture of Kievan Rus'
leaves.defn: The church architecture of Kievan Rus' and its successor principalities (10th–13th century): Saint Sophia Cathedral, Kyiv, Saint Sophia, Novgorod, the Church of the Intercession on the Nerl.

leaves.label: Armenian Architecture
leaves.defn: The stone church architecture of Armenia from the 4th century, with domed central plans and carved khachkars: Etchmiadzin Cathedral, Zvartnots, the Cathedral of the Holy Cross, Aghtamar.
leaves.aliases: Architecture of Armenia; Armenian church architecture
leaves.see: K4-6 Architecture of Georgia; K4-2 Byzantine Architecture

leaves.label: Architecture of Georgia
leaves.defn: The medieval church and fortress architecture of Georgia (Caucasus): Jvari, Svetitskhoveli, Bagrati Cathedral.

leaves.label: Pre-Romanesque Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of western Europe between the end of Rome and c. 1000: Visigothic, Asturian, Anglo-Saxon, Lombard and Mozarabic churches: Santa María del Naranco, San Juan de Baños, Escomb Church.
leaves.see: K4-8 Carolingian Architecture; K4-9 Ottonian Architecture; K4-10 Romanesque Architecture

leaves.label: Carolingian Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of the Carolingian empire (c. 780–900), reviving Roman forms: the Palatine Chapel, Aachen, the Lorsch gatehouse, Germigny-des-Prés.
leaves.see: K4-7 Pre-Romanesque Architecture; K4-9 Ottonian Architecture

leaves.label: Ottonian Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of the Ottonian empire (c. 936–1056) leading into Romanesque: St. Michael's Church, Hildesheim, St. Cyriakus, Gernrode.
leaves.see: K4-8 Carolingian Architecture; K4-10 Romanesque Architecture

leaves.label: Romanesque Architecture
leaves.defn: The round-arched, massive-walled architecture of Europe c. 1000–1200, with its regional schools: Speyer Cathedral, Sainte-Foy, Conques, Durham Cathedral, Pisa Cathedral.
leaves.see: K4-7 Pre-Romanesque Architecture; T181 Gothic Architecture; K2-8 Romanesque Revival Architecture

leaves.label: Arab-Norman Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of Norman Sicily (1091–1194) combining Latin, Byzantine and Islamic forms: the Palatine Chapel, Palermo, Monreale Cathedral, the Zisa.
leaves.see: K4-10 Romanesque Architecture; K1-3 Fatimid Architecture
leaves.weak: enwiki: Norman–Arab–Byzantine culture; label as in UNESCO WHS 1487 Arab-Norman Palermo; enwiki Arab-Norman architecture checked: no article; 27 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

leaves.label: Moldavian Style
leaves.defn: The church architecture of medieval Moldavia (15th–16th century), Gothic-Byzantine in plan with painted exteriors: Voroneț, Sucevița, Putna Monastery.
leaves.see: K4-2 Byzantine Architecture; K5-8 Brâncovenesc Style

leaves.label: Gothic Architecture
leaves.defn: Medieval European architecture of the pointed arch, rib vault and flying buttress (c. 1140–1520): Chartres Cathedral, Sainte-Chapelle, Cologne Cathedral.

subs.label: Early Modern European & Colonial Architecture
subs.axis: Axis: period style (Renaissance, Baroque, Rococo, Neoclassicism, Palladianism) and its colonial forms.

leaves.label: Tudor Architecture
leaves.defn: The English architecture of 1485–1603, late Perpendicular Gothic turning to Renaissance: Hampton Court Palace, King's College Chapel, Hardwick Hall.
leaves.see: T182 Renaissance Architecture; K2-7 Tudor Revival Architecture

leaves.label: Plateresque
leaves.defn: The Spanish style of c. 1490–1560 covering façades in fine silversmith-like Renaissance ornament: the University of Salamanca façade, San Esteban, Salamanca, Acolman.
leaves.see: T182 Renaissance Architecture; K5-4 Herrerian Style; K5-5 Churrigueresque

leaves.label: Manueline
leaves.defn: The Portuguese late Gothic style of the reign of Manuel I (1495–1521), with maritime and twisted-rope ornament: Jerónimos Monastery, Belém Tower, the Convent of Christ, Tomar.

leaves.label: Herrerian Style
leaves.defn: The austere classical style of Juan de Herrera for Philip II (from 1567): El Escorial, Valladolid Cathedral, the Archivo de Indias.

leaves.label: Churrigueresque
leaves.defn: The late Baroque style of Spain and New Spain (c. 1700–1760) with estípite pilasters and dense ornament: the Sagrario Metropolitano, Mexico City, the Transparente, Toledo.
leaves.see: T183 Baroque Architecture; K5-17 Andean Baroque

leaves.label: Rococo Architecture
leaves.defn: The late Baroque architecture and interior style of c. 1730–1770, light, asymmetrical and ornamental: Sanssouci, the Wieskirche, the Amalienburg.
leaves.see: T183 Baroque Architecture; T184 Neoclassical Architecture

leaves.label: Uzorochye
leaves.defn: The ornate Muscovite church and palace architecture of the 17th century, with tented roofs, kokoshniki and tilework: the Church of the Nativity in Putinki, the churches of Yaroslavl.
leaves.see: K4-4 Architecture of Kievan Rus'; K2-27 Russian Revival Architecture

leaves.label: Brâncovenesc Style
leaves.defn: The Wallachian style of Constantin Brâncoveanu's reign (1688–1714) combining Renaissance, Baroque and Ottoman elements: Horezu Monastery, Mogoșoaia Palace.
leaves.see: K4-12 Moldavian Style; K2-29 Romanian Revival Architecture

leaves.label: Palladian Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture derived from Andrea Palladio's villas and treatise, revived in 18th-century Britain, Ireland and America: Villa Rotonda, Chiswick House, Monticello.
leaves.see: T182 Renaissance Architecture; K5-10 Georgian Architecture

leaves.label: Georgian Architecture
leaves.defn: The British and colonial American classical architecture of 1714–1830, in brick and stone terraces, houses and churches: the Royal Crescent, Bath, Merrion Square, colonial Williamsburg.
leaves.see: K5-9 Palladian Architecture; K5-12 Federal Architecture; K2-21 Colonial Revival Architecture

leaves.label: Empire Style
leaves.defn: The Napoleonic phase of Neoclassicism (c. 1800–1830), spread across Europe and Russia: the Arc de Triomphe du Carrousel, La Madeleine, the Russian Empire buildings of St Petersburg.

leaves.label: Federal Architecture
leaves.defn: The American classical architecture of c. 1780–1830, after Adam and Palladio: the White House, Massachusetts State House, the Gardner–Pingree House.
leaves.see: K5-10 Georgian Architecture; K2-14 Greek Revival Architecture

leaves.label: Pombaline Style
leaves.defn: The rational, earthquake-resistant style of the rebuilding of Lisbon after 1755: the Baixa Pombalina, Praça do Comércio.

leaves.label: Architecture of the Bulgarian Revival
leaves.defn: The Bulgarian urban houses, churches and schools of the National Revival (18th–19th century): Plovdiv Old Town, Koprivshtitsa, the Rila Monastery's residential wings.

leaves.label: American Colonial Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of the English colonies of North America (17th–18th century): First Period timber houses, saltbox and Cape Cod types, Georgian brick: the Paul Revere House, Westover Plantation.
leaves.see: K5-10 Georgian Architecture; K5-20 Dutch Colonial Architecture; K2-21 Colonial Revival Architecture

leaves.label: Spanish Colonial Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of the Spanish empire in the Americas and the Philippines (16th–19th century): missions, cathedrals and plazas: the Mission San Xavier del Bac, Cusco Cathedral, the Baroque churches of the Philippines.
leaves.see: K5-17 Andean Baroque; K5-5 Churrigueresque; K2-22 Spanish Colonial Revival Architecture

leaves.label: Andean Baroque
leaves.defn: The mestizo Baroque of the colonial Andes (c. 1680–1780) with flat carved Indigenous-inflected ornament: San Lorenzo, Potosí, the Jesuit Church of Arequipa.
leaves.see: K5-16 Spanish Colonial Architecture; K5-5 Churrigueresque

leaves.label: Portuguese Colonial Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of the Portuguese empire in Brazil, Africa and Asia (16th–19th century): the historic centre of Ouro Preto, Salvador's Pelourinho, the churches of Old Goa.

leaves.label: French Colonial Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of the French colonies in North America and the Caribbean: raised galleried Creole houses and Quebec stone houses: the Bolduc House, the French Quarter, New Orleans.

leaves.label: Dutch Colonial Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of the Dutch colonies (New Netherland, the East Indies, Suriname), with gambrel and stepped-gable roofs: the Jan Martense Schenck House, Dutch colonial houses of Batavia.
leaves.see: K5-21 Cape Dutch Architecture; K5-15 American Colonial Architecture

leaves.label: Cape Dutch Architecture
leaves.defn: The whitewashed, thatched, ornate-gabled farmhouses of the Dutch Cape Colony (17th–18th century): Groot Constantia, Vergelegen.

leaves.label: Renaissance Architecture
leaves.defn: European architecture c. 1400–1600 reviving classical orders: Brunelleschi's Duomo dome, Bramante's Tempietto, Palladio's Villa Rotonda.

leaves.label: Baroque Architecture
leaves.defn: European and colonial architecture c. 1600–1750 of movement and spatial drama: Borromini's San Carlo, Versailles, Melk Abbey.

leaves.label: Neoclassical Architecture
leaves.defn: Architecture c. 1750–1850 on Greek and Roman models: the Panthéon, Paris, the British Museum, the Brandenburg Gate.

subs.label: Modern & Contemporary Architecture
subs.axis: Axis: movement (Art Nouveau, Modernism, Art Deco, Brutalism, Postmodernism, Deconstructivism).

leaves.label: Arts and Crafts Architecture
leaves.defn: The domestic architecture of the Arts and Crafts movement (c. 1860–1920), vernacular materials and honest craftsmanship: the Red House, Voysey's Broadleys, the Gamble House.
leaves.aliases: Arts and Crafts movement; Domestic Revival
leaves.see: T185 Art Nouveau Architecture; K6-3 Prairie School

leaves.label: Chicago School
leaves.defn: The steel-frame commercial architecture of Chicago (1880s–1910s), the first skyscrapers: the Home Insurance Building, the Monadnock Building, the Carson Pirie Scott Building.
leaves.see: K6-3 Prairie School; T186 Modern Architecture

leaves.label: Prairie School
leaves.defn: The Midwestern American architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright and his circle (c. 1900–1917), low and horizontal: Robie House, Unity Temple, the Darwin D. Martin House.
leaves.see: K6-2 Chicago School; K6-1 Arts and Crafts Architecture

leaves.label: Czech Cubism
leaves.defn: The Cubist architecture of Bohemia (1910–1925), with faceted crystalline façades and its later rondocubist phase: the House of the Black Madonna, the Kovařovic Villa, the Adria Palace.
leaves.see: K6-5 Expressionist Architecture; T185 Art Nouveau Architecture

leaves.label: Expressionist Architecture
leaves.defn: The early 20th-century European architecture of distorted, sculptural and crystalline form, in brick and concrete: the Einstein Tower, the Chilehaus, Het Schip.
leaves.see: T186 Modern Architecture; K6-4 Czech Cubism

leaves.label: Futurist Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of speed and the machine announced by Sant'Elia (1914) and its later heirs, from Googie to neo-futurism: Sant'Elia's Città Nuova, the Theme Building, LAX.
leaves.see: K6-5 Expressionist Architecture; K6-19 High-tech Architecture

leaves.label: Art Deco Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of Art Deco (c. 1920–1940), geometric, stepped and ornamented, with its Streamline Moderne phase: the Chrysler Building, Miami Beach's Art Deco District, Napier.
leaves.see: T185 Art Nouveau Architecture; T186 Modern Architecture; K6-14 Stripped Classicism

leaves.label: Bauhaus Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of the Bauhaus school and its masters (1919–1933) and its diaspora: the Bauhaus Dessau, the Masters' Houses, Tel Aviv's White City.
leaves.see: K6-9 International Style; T186 Modern Architecture

leaves.label: International Style
leaves.defn: The modern architecture named by Hitchcock and Johnson (1932): volume rather than mass, regularity, no applied ornament: Villa Savoye, the Barcelona Pavilion, the Seagram Building.
leaves.see: K6-8 Bauhaus Architecture; T186 Modern Architecture; K6-18 Mid-Century Modern Architecture

leaves.label: Constructivist Architecture
leaves.defn: The Soviet avant-garde architecture of the 1920s–early 1930s: the Shukhov Tower, the Narkomfin Building, the Rusakov Workers' Club.
leaves.see: T186 Modern Architecture; K6-15 Stalinist Architecture

leaves.label: Reform Architecture
leaves.defn: The German-speaking reform movement of c. 1900–1930 that rejected historicism for simple, regional building (Heimatschutz, Um 1800): Paul Schultze-Naumburg's Cecilienhof, Hellerau.
leaves.see: T186 Modern Architecture; K6-12 Traditionalist School

leaves.label: Traditionalist School
leaves.defn: The Dutch traditionalist architecture of c. 1900–1960 in brick and tile, with its Delft and Bossche schools: Granpré Molière's Vreewijk, Dom Hans van der Laan's Roosenberg Abbey.
leaves.see: K6-11 Reform Architecture; K6-5 Expressionist Architecture

leaves.label: Nordic Classicism
leaves.defn: The pared-down classical architecture of Scandinavia and Finland c. 1910–1930: Asplund's Stockholm City Library, the Woodland Chapel, Aalto's early Jyväskylä buildings.
leaves.see: K6-14 Stripped Classicism; K6-9 International Style

leaves.label: Stripped Classicism
leaves.defn: The simplified, unornamented classicism of the 1920s–1940s for government buildings in democracies and dictatorships alike: the Federal Reserve Board Building, the Palais de Chaillot.
leaves.see: K6-13 Nordic Classicism; K6-15 Stalinist Architecture; K6-16 Fascist Architecture

leaves.label: Stalinist Architecture
leaves.defn: The monumental socialist-realist architecture of the USSR and its satellites (1933–1955): the Seven Sisters, the Palace of Culture and Science, Karl-Marx-Allee.
leaves.see: K6-10 Constructivist Architecture; K6-14 Stripped Classicism; K6-16 Fascist Architecture

leaves.label: Fascist Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of Fascist Italy (1922–1943), from rationalism to monumental stripped classicism: EUR, Rome, the Casa del Fascio, Como, the Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana.
leaves.aliases: Stile Littorio; architecture of the Fascist period
leaves.see: K6-17 Nazi Architecture; K6-14 Stripped Classicism; T186 Modern Architecture

leaves.label: Nazi Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of the Third Reich (1933–1945), monumental neoclassical for the state and Heimatstil for housing: the Nuremberg Rally Grounds, Tempelhof Airport, the Reich Chancellery.
leaves.see: K6-16 Fascist Architecture; K6-15 Stalinist Architecture

leaves.label: Mid-Century Modern Architecture
leaves.defn: The American-led domestic and commercial modernism of c. 1945–1970: post-and-beam houses, glass pavilions and regional variants: the Eames House, the Stahl House, Miami Modern hotels.
leaves.see: K6-9 International Style; T187 Brutalist Architecture

leaves.label: High-tech Architecture
leaves.defn: Late-modern architecture from the 1970s that expresses structure and services as industrial technology: the Centre Pompidou, the Lloyd's Building, HSBC Main Building, Hong Kong.
leaves.see: T188 Postmodern Architecture; T190 Contemporary Architecture

leaves.label: New Classical Architecture
leaves.defn: Contemporary classical and traditional architecture since the 1980s: Poundbury, Robert Adam's Sackler Library, the Schermerhorn Symphony Center.
leaves.see: T188 Postmodern Architecture; T184 Neoclassical Architecture

leaves.label: Art Nouveau Architecture
leaves.defn: Architecture of the Art Nouveau c. 1890–1914: Horta's Hôtel Tassel, Guimard's Métro entrances, Gaudí's Casa Batlló.

leaves.label: Modern Architecture
leaves.defn: Architecture of the modern movement (c. 1900–1975): functionalism, the International Style and their regional forms: Villa Savoye, the Barcelona Pavilion, Fallingwater.

leaves.label: Brutalist Architecture
leaves.defn: Modernist architecture of the 1950s–1970s in exposed concrete and massive forms: Unité d'Habitation, the Barbican Estate, Boston City Hall.

leaves.label: Postmodern Architecture
leaves.defn: Architecture from the 1960s–1990s returning to ornament, history and irony: Venturi's Vanna Venturi House, Graves's Portland Building, Stirling's Neue Staatsgalerie.

leaves.label: Deconstructivism
leaves.defn: Architecture from the 1980s of fragmented, non-rectilinear forms: Gehry's Guggenheim Bilbao, Libeskind's Jewish Museum Berlin, Hadid's Vitra Fire Station.

leaves.label: Contemporary Architecture
leaves.defn: Architecture by architects born from 1945, in plural idioms from parametric design to vernacular-sustainable building: Kéré's Gando school, SANAA's Rolex Learning Center.

subs.label: South Asian Architecture
subs.axis: Axis: temple and building tradition (Nagara, Dravidian, Vesara, Buddhist, Indo-Islamic outside K1).

leaves.label: Nagara Architecture
leaves.defn: The northern Hindu and Jain temple tradition whose sanctum rises in a curvilinear shikhara of stacked courses (latina, shekhari and bhumija forms): Kandariya Mahadeva at Khajuraho, Mahabodhi Temple, Kopeshwar temple, Khidrapur.
leaves.aliases: Nagara style;North Indian temple architecture;Indo-Aryan temple style
leaves.see: K7-2 Kalinga Architecture; K7-3 Maru-Gurjara Architecture; K7-5 Vesara

leaves.label: Kalinga Architecture
leaves.defn: The Odishan temple tradition of the rekha, pidha and khakhara deula with jagamohana halls (7th–13th century): Lingaraja Temple, Konark Sun Temple, Jagannath Temple, Puri.
leaves.see: K7-1 Nagara Architecture; K7-7 Bengal Temple Architecture

leaves.label: Maru-Gurjara Architecture
leaves.defn: The temple tradition of Gujarat and Rajasthan (11th–13th century and its revival) with richly carved marble interiors, especially for Jain patrons: Dilwara temples, Mount Abu, Modhera Sun Temple, Ranakpur.

leaves.label: Dravidian Architecture
leaves.defn: The southern Hindu temple tradition of stepped pyramidal vimanas, pillared mandapas and monumental gopurams in walled precincts: Shore Temple, Mahabalipuram, Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur, Meenakshi Temple, Madurai, Virupaksha Temple, Hampi.
leaves.aliases: Dravida style;South Indian temple architecture;Tamil architecture;kovil

leaves.label: Vesara
leaves.defn: The Deccan temple tradition combining Nagara and Dravidian forms, developed under the Chalukyas and Hoysalas: Pattadakal, Mahadeva Temple, Itagi, Chennakesava Temple, Belur, Hoysaleswara Temple, Halebidu.
leaves.see: K7-4 Dravidian Architecture; K7-1 Nagara Architecture

leaves.label: Kerala Architecture
leaves.defn: The timber-and-laterite building tradition of Kerala with steep tiled and copper roofs: circular and rectangular sreekovil temples, koothambalam theatres, nalukettu houses and palaces: Vadakkunnathan Temple, Padmanabhapuram Palace, Mattancherry Palace.

leaves.label: Bengal Temple Architecture
leaves.defn: The brick and terracotta temples of Bengal (16th–19th century) whose curved roofs translate the thatched hut: the chala types (do-chala, char-chala, at-chala), jor-bangla and the ratna (pinnacled) types: Jor Bangla Temple, Bishnupur, Rasmancha, Dakshineswar Kali Temple.
leaves.aliases: Bengal temple style;terracotta temples of Bengal

leaves.label: Buddhist Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of Buddhism in its South Asian homeland: stupas, chaitya halls and vihara monasteries from the Mauryas to the Palas, and the monasteries of Gandhara: Great Stupa, Sanchi, Dhamek Stupa, Nalanda Mahavihara, Takht-i-Bahi.
leaves.see: K7-9 Indian Rock-cut Architecture; K7-10 Sinhalese Architecture; K7-12 Tibetan Buddhist Architecture

leaves.label: Indian Rock-cut Architecture
leaves.defn: Caves, halls and monolithic temples excavated from living rock (3rd century BCE–10th century): Ajanta Caves, Karla chaitya, Kailasa Temple, Ellora, Elephanta Caves.
leaves.see: K7-8 Buddhist Architecture; K7-4 Dravidian Architecture

leaves.label: Sinhalese Architecture
leaves.defn: The Buddhist and royal architecture of Sri Lanka: dagobas, vatadages, image houses and monasteries of Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa, and the timber halls of the Kandyan kingdom: Ruwanweli Maha Seya, Jetavanaramaya, Gal Vihara, Temple of the Tooth.
leaves.aliases: architecture of Sri Lanka;Sri Lankan Buddhist architecture
leaves.weak: attested through the article on the architecture of Sri Lanka (no article under the Sinhalese label)

leaves.label: Newar Architecture
leaves.defn: The brick-and-timber architecture of the Newars of the Kathmandu valley: multi-roofed pagoda temples, shikhara temples, stupas, bahal courtyards and palace squares with carved struts and windows: Pashupatinath, Nyatapola, Changu Narayan, Swayambhunath.
leaves.see: K7-12 Tibetan Buddhist Architecture; K7-1 Nagara Architecture

leaves.label: Tibetan Buddhist Architecture
leaves.defn: The monastic and palace architecture of Tibet and the Tibetan Buddhist world: battered stone-and-earth walls, flat roofs, gilded roofs, chortens and kumbums: Potala Palace, Jokhang, Drepung, Gyantse Kumbum.
leaves.see: K7-13 Dzong Architecture; K7-11 Newar Architecture

leaves.label: Dzong Architecture
leaves.defn: The fortress-monasteries of Bhutan and Tibet housing civil and monastic administration around a central utse tower: Punakha Dzong, Paro Rinpung Dzong, Trongsa Dzong.

leaves.label: Rajput Architecture
leaves.defn: The forts, palaces, havelis and cenotaphs of the Rajput kingdoms of Rajasthan and Central India (8th–19th century), with jharokhas and chhatris: Amber Fort, Chittorgarh Fort, Kumbhalgarh, Jaisalmer Fort.

leaves.label: Stepwell
leaves.defn: The stepped subterranean wells of western India built as civic and devotional monuments, Hindu and Islamic (vav, baoli): Rani ki vav, Adalaj Stepwell, Chand Baori.

leaves.label: Sikh Architecture
leaves.defn: The gurdwaras and memorials of the Sikh tradition (17th–19th century) drawing on Mughal and Rajput forms, with fluted domes and gilded upper storeys: Harmandir Sahib, Takht Sri Patna Sahib, Gurdwara Baba Atal.

leaves.label: Harappan Architecture
leaves.defn: The planned fired-brick cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation (c. 2600–1900 BCE): grid streets, drains, granaries and citadels: Great Bath, Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira.

leaves.label: Chinese Architecture
leaves.defn: The classical timber-frame tradition of China, with bracket sets (dougong), raised platforms and sweeping tiled roofs, used for palaces, altars, temples, pagodas and gateways and codified in official manuals (Yingzao Fashi): Forbidden City, Temple of Heaven, Foguang Temple, Giant Wild Goose Pagoda.
leaves.see: K8-2 Siheyuan; K8-20 Korean Architecture; K8-11 Japanese Buddhist Architecture

leaves.label: Siheyuan
leaves.defn: The north-Chinese courtyard house of four halls round a central yard, the model of the Beijing hutong: Prince Gong Mansion, Qiao Family Compound.

leaves.label: Yaodong
leaves.defn: The earth-sheltered cave dwellings of the Loess Plateau, cut into cliffs, sunk round pit courtyards or built as vaults.

leaves.label: Hakka Walled Village
leaves.defn: The fortified communal dwellings of the Hakka and Minnan of southern China: the earthen tulou of Fujian, weilongwu and walled villages: Tianluokeng tulou cluster, Chengqi Lou.
leaves.see: K8-7 Hokkien Architecture; K8-6 Lingnan Architecture

leaves.label: Hui-style Architecture
leaves.defn: The merchant houses, ancestral halls and memorial arches of Huizhou (southern Anhui), with whitewashed walls, stepped horse-head gables and carved brick, wood and stone: Xidi, Hongcun.

leaves.label: Lingnan Architecture
leaves.defn: The building tradition of Guangdong and Guangxi: wok-ear gables, ceramic ridge figures, arcaded qilou shophouses and Lingnan gardens: Chen Clan Ancestral Hall, Foshan Ancestral Temple.
leaves.see: K8-7 Hokkien Architecture; K8-4 Hakka Walled Village

leaves.label: Hokkien Architecture
leaves.defn: The Minnan building tradition of southern Fujian, Taiwan and the Hokkien diaspora: swallowtail ridges, red brick and cut-porcelain (jian nian) roof decoration on temples and houses: Bangka Lungshan Temple, Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou.
leaves.see: K8-6 Lingnan Architecture; K8-4 Hakka Walled Village

leaves.label: Sichuanese Architecture
leaves.defn: The timber and stilted vernacular of Sichuan and Chongqing (chuan-dou framing, diaojiaolou), with its Song–Yuan temple halls.
leaves.weak: weakly attested: a Wikidata item with no sitelinks; kept because of its heritage buildings

leaves.label: Shikumen
leaves.defn: The Shanghai lane-house (lilong) type of the 1860s–1930s joining a Chinese courtyard plan to Western terrace housing behind stone-framed gates: Xintiandi, Tianzifang.

leaves.label: Shinto Shrine Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of Japanese Shinto shrines (jinja) in named styles (zukuri) defined by roof, entrance and plan: Ise Grand Shrine (shinmei), Izumo Taisha (taisha), Kamigamo Shrine (nagare), Nikkō Tōshō-gū (gongen).

leaves.label: Japanese Buddhist Architecture
leaves.defn: The temple architecture of Japanese Buddhism in its named styles: wayō, daibutsuyō, zenshūyō and the mixed setchūyō, with pagodas, halls, gates and storehouses: Hōryū-ji, Tōdai-ji, Byōdō-in, Engaku-ji Shariden.
leaves.see: K8-10 Shinto Shrine Architecture; K8-1 Chinese Architecture

leaves.label: Shinden-zukuri
leaves.defn: The Heian aristocratic residence of a main hall facing a south garden and pond, linked to wings by corridors: Kyoto Imperial Palace Shishinden, Byōdō-in (derived).

leaves.label: Shoin-zukuri
leaves.defn: The warrior-class residential style of the Muromachi to Edo periods with tatami rooms, tokonoma alcove, staggered shelves, built-in desk and sliding fusuma: Ninomaru Palace, Nijō Castle, Kojō-in, Onjō-ji.

leaves.label: Sukiya-zukuri
leaves.defn: The informal residential and tea-house style derived from the chashitsu, using natural materials and restrained finish: Katsura Imperial Villa, Tai-an, Jo-an.

leaves.label: Minka
leaves.defn: The vernacular houses of Japan's farmers, craftsmen and merchants: farmhouses (nōka) and townhouses (machiya), in regional types such as gasshō-zukuri and magariya: Shirakawa-gō, Kyoto machiya.

leaves.label: Japanese Castle Architecture
leaves.defn: The fortified residences of the daimyō (16th–17th century): stone ramparts, moats, gates and the multi-storey tenshu keep: Himeji Castle, Matsumoto Castle, Osaka Castle.

leaves.label: Kofun
leaves.defn: The mounded tombs of Japan's Kofun period (3rd–7th century), above all the keyhole-shaped zenpō-kōen-fun, often moated and set with haniwa: Daisen Kofun, Mozu-Furuichi kofun group, Ishibutai Kofun.

leaves.label: Ryukyuan Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of the Ryukyu kingdom (Okinawa): red-tiled gusuku castles and palaces, utaki sacred groves and turtleback and gable-roofed tombs: Shuri Castle, Tamaudun, Nakagusuku Castle.

leaves.label: Giyōfū Architecture
leaves.defn: The pseudo-Western buildings of early Meiji Japan (1860s–1880s) made by Japanese carpenters imitating Western forms in timber and plaster: Former Kaichi School, Tsukiji Hotel, Former Saiseikan Hospital.

leaves.label: Korean Architecture
leaves.defn: The timber-frame architecture of Korea's palaces, temples, shrines and fortresses, classified by bracket system (jusimpo, dapo, ikgong) and painted in dancheong: Gyeongbokgung, Bulguksa, Jongmyo, Haeinsa Janggyeong Panjeon.
leaves.see: K8-21 Hanok; K8-1 Chinese Architecture; K7-2 Dancheong

leaves.label: Hanok
leaves.defn: The traditional Korean house with ondol-heated rooms, wooden maru floors and tiled or thatched roofs, set by geomancy: Bukchon Hanok Village, Hahoe Folk Village, Yangdong Village.

subs.label: Southeast Asian Architecture
subs.axis: Axis: building tradition (Khmer, Javanese, Burmese, Thai, Cham).

leaves.label: Khmer Architecture
leaves.defn: The temple-mountains, galleried enclosures and prasat towers of the Khmer empire and its predecessors (7th–13th century) in successive named styles (Sambor Prei Kuk, Preah Ko, Bakheng, Banteay Srei, Baphuon, Angkor Wat, Bayon): Angkor Wat, Banteay Srei, Bayon, Preah Vihear.
leaves.see: K9-8 Cham Architecture; K9-6 Thai Architecture

leaves.label: Candi Architecture
leaves.defn: The Hindu and Buddhist stone temples and stupas of classical Indonesia (7th–15th century), in the Central Javanese (Mataram) and East Javanese (Singhasari, Majapahit) styles and in Sumatra: Borobudur, Prambanan, Candi Penataran, Muara Takus.

leaves.label: Balinese Architecture
leaves.defn: The Hindu-Balinese building tradition of walled pura temples with split gates (candi bentar), meru towers and pavilions, and compound houses laid out by cosmological axes: Pura Besakih, Pura Taman Ayun, Pura Ulun Danu Bratan.
leaves.see: K9-2 Candi Architecture; K9-4 Javanese Traditional House

leaves.label: Javanese Traditional House
leaves.defn: The timber houses of Java in ranked roof types (joglo, limasan, kampung) with the open pendopo pavilion in front: Kraton Yogyakarta pendopo, Mangkunegaran Palace.

leaves.label: Burmese Architecture
leaves.defn: The Buddhist architecture of Myanmar: bell-shaped zedi stupas, hollow gu temples, pyatthat spires and teak monasteries, from Pagan to Mandalay: Ananda Temple, Shwezigon, Shwedagon Pagoda, Shwenandaw Monastery.

leaves.label: Thai Architecture
leaves.defn: The Buddhist and royal architecture of Thailand, in the art-historical styles of Sukhothai, Lanna, Ayutthaya and Rattanakosin: wat compounds with ubosot, vihara, chedi, prang and mondop: Wat Mahathat, Sukhothai, Wat Phra Si Sanphet, Wat Phrathat Doi Suthep, Wat Phra Kaew.
leaves.see: K9-1 Khmer Architecture; K9-7 Lao Architecture; K9-5 Burmese Architecture

leaves.label: Lao Architecture
leaves.defn: The Buddhist architecture of Laos (Lan Xang) in the Luang Prabang, Vientiane and Xieng Khouang temple styles with sweeping multi-tiered roofs and that stupas: Wat Xieng Thong, Pha That Luang, Wat Si Saket.
leaves.weak: WEAK: no English article on Lao architecture (Architecture of Laos redirects to Culture of Laos); attested through UNESCO Town of Luang Prabang, which describes the traditional Lao temple architecture

leaves.label: Cham Architecture
leaves.defn: The brick tower-temples (kalan) of the Champa kingdoms in central and southern Vietnam (7th–15th century) in successive styles (Mỹ Sơn E1, Đồng Dương, Tháp Mắm): Mỹ Sơn, Po Nagar, Po Klong Garai.
leaves.see: K9-1 Khmer Architecture; K9-9 Vietnamese Architecture

leaves.label: Vietnamese Architecture
leaves.defn: The timber architecture of Vietnam's pagodas (chùa), communal houses (đình), citadels and imperial tombs, from the Lý to the Nguyễn: One Pillar Pagoda, Temple of Literature, Thiên Mụ Pagoda, Imperial City of Huế.
leaves.see: K9-8 Cham Architecture; K8-1 Chinese Architecture

leaves.label: Batak Architecture
leaves.defn: The saddle-roofed timber houses (rumah adat) and granaries of the Batak peoples of North Sumatra, raised on piles and carved and painted with gorga ornament.

leaves.label: Bahay Kubo
leaves.defn: The Philippine nipa hut: a stilted house of bamboo and timber with a thatched nipa roof, the base type of lowland Filipino vernacular.

leaves.label: Bahay na Bato
leaves.defn: The Spanish-colonial Filipino town house (18th–19th century) with a stone lower storey and a timber upper storey with capiz-shell sliding windows: Vigan, Casa Manila.

leaves.label: Sino-Portuguese Architecture
leaves.defn: The shophouses and mansions of Phuket, Penang and the Straits Settlements (late 19th–early 20th century) mixing Hokkien plans with European façades.

subs.label: African Architecture
subs.axis: Axis: building tradition (Sudano-Sahelian, Ethiopian rock-hewn, Great Zimbabwe, Swahili).

leaves.label: Aksumite Architecture
leaves.defn: The stone architecture of the Aksumite kingdom (1st–7th century) with its 'monkey-head' timber-and-rubble walls, palaces and carved monolithic stelae: Northern Stelae Field, Aksum, Dungur palace, Debre Damo.
leaves.weak: the title is a redirect to Architecture of Ethiopia (section on Aksumite architecture)

leaves.label: Ethiopian Rock-hewn Churches
leaves.defn: The monolithic and semi-monolithic churches carved from rock in Ethiopia (10th–13th century and later): Bete Giyorgis, Lalibela, Bete Medhane Alem, Abuna Yemata Guh.
leaves.aliases: rock-hewn churches of Lalibela;Tigray rock churches
leaves.see: K10-1 Aksumite Architecture; K10-3 Gondarine Architecture

leaves.label: Gondarine Architecture
leaves.defn: The castle-palaces and churches of the Gondar period (17th–18th century), with battlemented towers and domes: Fasil Ghebbi, Fasilides' Bath, Debre Berhan Selassie.
leaves.weak: attested through the type site; no article under the style name

leaves.label: Nubian Pyramids
leaves.defn: The steep pyramids, temples and palaces of the Kushite kingdoms of Napata and Meroë (8th century BCE–4th century CE): Meroë, Jebel Barkal, El-Kurru, Musawwarat es-Sufra.

leaves.label: Great Zimbabwe
leaves.defn: The dry-stone architecture of the Zimbabwe culture (11th–19th century): mortarless granite enclosures, coursed walls with chevron and chequer friezes: Great Zimbabwe, Khami, Mapungubwe, Naletale.

leaves.label: Ksar
leaves.defn: The fortified earthen and stone villages, granaries (agadir, ghorfa) and kasbahs of the Amazigh and Saharan world: Aït Benhaddou, Ksar of Ouadane, Ksar Ouled Soltane, Ghardaïa (M'zab).

leaves.label: Hausa Architecture
leaves.defn: The earthen architecture of the Hausa city-states of northern Nigeria and Niger: domed and vaulted mud houses and palaces with relief façades (zanko pinnacles): Gidan Rumfa, Kano, Zaria Friday Mosque.

subs.label: Indigenous American Architecture
subs.axis: Axis: building tradition (Maya, Mesoamerican, Andean, Pueblo, Eastern Woodlands).

leaves.label: Maya Architecture
leaves.defn: The stone architecture of the Maya (c. 1000 BCE–1500 CE): stepped pyramid-temples, palaces with corbel vaults, ballcourts and stelae plazas, in the regional styles Petén, Usumacinta, Río Bec, Chenes and Puuc: Tikal Temple I, Temple of the Inscriptions, Palenque, Uxmal, Chichen Itza.
leaves.see: K11-2 Mesoamerican Architecture; K11-3 Aztec Architecture

leaves.label: Mesoamerican Architecture
leaves.defn: The monumental architecture of non-Maya Mesoamerica: Olmec mounds, the talud-tablero platforms of Teotihuacan, Zapotec and Mixtec Oaxaca, Classic Veracruz and Toltec Tula: Pyramid of the Sun, Monte Albán, Mitla, Pyramid of the Niches, El Tajín.
leaves.see: K11-1 Maya Architecture; K11-3 Aztec Architecture

leaves.label: Aztec Architecture
leaves.defn: The architecture of the Mexica and their Late Postclassic neighbours (14th–16th century): twin-temple pyramids, palaces and causeway cities: Templo Mayor, Tenayuca, Santa Cecilia Acatitlan, Malinalco.

leaves.label: Inca Architecture
leaves.defn: The fitted-masonry architecture of Tawantinsuyu (15th–16th century): ashlar and polygonal walls, trapezoidal doorways and niches, terraces, roads and tambos: Machu Picchu, Sacsayhuamán, Coricancha, Ollantaytambo.

leaves.label: Andean Architecture
leaves.defn: The monumental architecture of the Andes before the Inca: Caral's platform mounds, Chavín's galleried temple, Moche adobe huacas, Tiwanaku's stone platforms, Wari administrative centres, Chimú Chan Chan and Chachapoya Kuélap.
leaves.weak: WEAK: no English article titled Andean architecture for the pre-Inca building traditions; attested through the Andean civilizations article; cultures are kinds

leaves.label: Ancestral Puebloan Architecture
leaves.defn: The masonry and adobe great houses, cliff dwellings, kivas and terraced pueblos of the Ancestral Puebloans and their descendants in the US Southwest: Pueblo Bonito, Chaco Canyon, Cliff Palace, Mesa Verde, Taos Pueblo.

leaves.label: Mound Builders
leaves.defn: The earthen platform mounds, effigy mounds and geometric earthworks of the Eastern Woodlands (Archaic to Mississippian, c. 3500 BCE–1600 CE): Poverty Point, Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks, Monks Mound, Cahokia, Serpent Mound.

subs.label: Vernacular & Oceanic Architecture
subs.axis: Axis: building tradition (named vernacular styles, Pacific meeting houses).

leaves.label: Wharenui
leaves.defn: The carved Māori meeting house on the marae, its frame read as the body of an ancestor: Te Hau ki Tūranga, Te Tokanganui-a-Noho, Rauru.

leaves.label: Fale
leaves.defn: The Samoan open-sided house with a domed thatched roof on posts, including the round fale tele guest house.

leaves.label: Maneaba
leaves.defn: The great community meeting house of Kiribati and Tuvalu, a vast thatched roof on low posts.

leaves.label: Haus Tambaran
leaves.defn: The spirit and men's houses of the Sepik region of Papua New Guinea with soaring painted gable façades.

leaves.label: Marae
leaves.defn: The stone-paved ceremonial platforms and courts of East Polynesia, including the image ahu of Rapa Nui with their moai: Taputapuātea, Ahu Tongariki, Ahu Tahai.

leaves.label: Nan Madol
leaves.defn: The basalt-prism megalithic architecture of the Saudeleur polity on Pohnpei (c. 1180–1628) and Leluh on Kosrae: artificial islets of stacked columnar basalt.

leaves.label: Chilotan Architecture
leaves.defn: The shingled timber architecture of the Chiloé archipelago, above all the Jesuit-founded wooden churches built by local boatwrights (18th–19th century): Church of Castro, Church of Achao, palafitos of Castro.
leaves.aliases: Chiloé School of religious wooden architecture

subs.label: Gardens & Designed Landscapes
subs.axis: Axis: garden tradition (Persian chahar bagh, Chinese scholar garden, Japanese garden, Italian Renaissance, French formal, English landscape).

leaves.label: Persian Garden
leaves.defn: The walled garden of Iran laid out as a chahar bagh, four plots divided by water channels around a pavilion, from Achaemenid Pasargadae to the Safavid and Qajar gardens (UNESCO 2011): Pasargadae, Bagh-e Fin, Kashan, Eram Garden, Shiraz, Shazdeh Garden, Mahan.
leaves.weak: 'Persian garden' redirects to Persian gardens; Charbagh has its own article (kind)

leaves.label: Mughal Garden
leaves.defn: The gardens of the Mughal emperors in South Asia, 16th–18th century, built on the chahar bagh with terraces, cascades and tomb or pleasure pavilions: Humayun's Tomb garden, Taj Mahal charbagh, Shalimar Bagh, Srinagar, Shalimar Gardens, Lahore.

leaves.label: Chinese Garden
leaves.defn: The Chinese classical garden of rocks, water, pavilions and planting composed as a landscape in miniature, in its imperial and scholar's (literati) forms: Humble Administrator's Garden, Lingering Garden, Summer Palace, Yu Garden.
leaves.aliases: Chinese classical garden;scholar's garden;Chinese scholar garden;yuanlin
leaves.see: K13-4 Japanese Garden;A2-3 Literati Painting;K8 East Asian Architecture

leaves.label: Japanese Garden
leaves.defn: The Japanese garden tradition from the Heian pond garden through the Zen dry landscape and the tea garden to the Edo stroll garden: Ryōan-ji rock garden, Saihō-ji moss garden, Katsura Imperial Villa, Kenroku-en.

leaves.label: Italian Renaissance Garden
leaves.defn: The terraced villa garden of 15th–16th-century Italy, ordered by axis and geometry with fountains, grottoes, statuary and giochi d'acqua: Villa d'Este, Tivoli, Boboli Gardens, Villa Lante, Bagnaia, Sacro Bosco, Bomarzo.
leaves.see: K13-6 French Formal Garden;K5 Early Modern European & Colonial Architecture

leaves.label: French Formal Garden
leaves.defn: The garden à la française of 17th-century France, a geometric composition of parterres, basins and long axes ordered from the château, perfected by André Le Nôtre: Vaux-le-Vicomte, Gardens of Versailles, Chantilly, Tuileries.
leaves.aliases: garden à la française;jardin à la française;French garden;formal garden
leaves.see: K13-5 Italian Renaissance Garden;K13-7 English Landscape Garden;I3-4 Louis XIV Style

leaves.label: English Landscape Garden
leaves.defn: The informal 'natural' landscape park of 18th-century Britain, with lawns, serpentine lakes, belts of trees and temples composed as pictures, and its picturesque and international offshoots: Stourhead, Stowe, Blenheim Park, Wörlitz Park.
leaves.aliases: English garden;English landscape park;jardin à l'anglaise;landscape garden
leaves.see: K13-6 French Formal Garden;K5 Early Modern European & Colonial Architecture

fams.label: Art in Place
fams.test: made on or into a fixed surface and studied where it stands — rock art, wall painting, in-situ mosaic and tile revetment, geoglyphs — or made on the living body.
key: 1. Pecked, engraved or painted on rock? → L1. 2. Painted on a wall or ceiling? → L2. 3. Mosaic, tile revetment or mirror work assembled on site? → L3. 4. A ground figure? → L4. 5. On the body (tattoo, body painting, henna)? → L5.
6. An ephemeral design drawn on a floor or the ground in powder, sand or paste? → L6.

leaves.label: Bhimbetka Rock Paintings
leaves.defn: Painted rock shelters of the Vindhyan hills from the Mesolithic to the historical period (UNESCO 2003): hunting scenes, dancers, Zoo Rock.

leaves.label: Petroglyphs of the Mongolian Altai
leaves.defn: The rock carvings and paintings of the Mongolian Altai (UNESCO 2011), from about 11,000 years ago to the Turkic period: Tsagaan Salaa, Upper Tsagaan Gol, Aral Tolgoi.
leaves.aliases: Petroglyphic Complexes of the Mongolian Altai

leaves.label: Tamgaly Petroglyphs
leaves.defn: The Bronze Age to medieval rock carvings of Tamgaly and the Semirechye (UNESCO 2004), with sun-headed figures and sacrificial scenes: sun-headed deities, bull and chariot scenes.

leaves.label: Maros-Pangkep Cave Art
leaves.defn: Painted and stencilled rock art of the limestone karst of South Sulawesi, among the oldest figurative art known (45,000+ years): Leang Tedongnge warty pig, Leang Bulu' Sipong 4 hunting scene, hand stencils.
src: Wikidata Q66023283 (Prehistoric Cave Sites in Maros-Pangkep)

leaves.label: Sangkulirang-Mangkalihat Rock Art
leaves.defn: Hand stencils and animal paintings of the limestone caves of East Kalimantan and of Niah in Sarawak: Lubang Jeriji Saléh banteng, Niah Painted Cave.

leaves.label: Zuojiang Huashan Rock Art
leaves.defn: Red-ochre rock paintings of the Luo Yue people on cliffs along the Zuojiang river in Guangxi (5th c. BCE–2nd c. CE), with figures and bronze drums (UNESCO 2016).

leaves.label: Bangudae Petroglyphs
leaves.defn: Neolithic and Bronze Age petroglyphs on the Daegok stream in Ulsan, with whales, hunters and boats, and the nearby Cheonjeon-ri carvings (UNESCO 2025).

leaves.label: Fugoppe Cave
leaves.defn: Incised figures and signs in the Fugoppe cave in Hokkaido (Epi-Jōmon) and the related Temiya cave carvings.

leaves.label: Helan Mountains Petroglyphs
leaves.defn: Petroglyphs pecked on the cliffs of the Helan and Yin mountains of Ningxia and Inner Mongolia, from the Neolithic to the medieval period: masks, animals and hunters (Helankou, Damaidi).

leaves.label: Saharan Rock Art
